questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: Governing by grant in the early Zhou
questions.learningObjective: Identify what a grant of land and people primarily secured for the Zhou king
questions.stem: An engineer's design brief asks which outcome a land grant in early Zhou most reliably secured for the king

options.text: A permanent, unconditional transfer of territory to the grantee with no duties attached
options.misconception: treats a grant as an outright gift with no obligations

options.text: A network of loyal kin who owed military service and tribute in return for the land
options.misconception: ignores the reciprocal duty that defined the grant

options.text: A mechanism binding regional lords to the king through mutual obligation
A simple record of tax revenue collected from peasants by central officials
options.misconception: confuses a political bond with a tax receipt

questions.explanation: The grant created mutual obligation between king and lord, not an unconditional gift. Option A misses the duties; B narrows it to kin only; D misreads the document as a tax record.
questions.hint: Think about what both sides gained and owed.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: Explain the duties a grant document imposed on the recipient
questions.stem: An engineer's design brief asks what duties a grant document imposed on the lord who received land and people

answer.exemplar: A grant document bound the recipient to provide military service, tribute, and loyalty to the king, while the king promised protection and recognition of the lord's authority over the granted territory and people.

questions.explanation: The document was a two-sided contract. The lord gained land and people but owed service and tribute; the king gained support but had to protect the lord.
questions.hint: Consider both sides of the agreement.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: Identify why early Zhou rulers inscribed questions on bone

stimulus.body: The king cracks a bone and asks whether the coming season will bring rain. The scribe records the crack and the answer. Later readers treat the bone as both question and record.

questions.stem: An engineer's design brief asks what function the bone inscription primarily served for the ruler

options.text: It recorded a question posed to ancestors or spirits and the resulting omen
It preserved a legal contract between the king and a regional lord
options.misconception: confuses divination with a legal grant

options.text: It listed the names of craftsmen who made bronze vessels
options.misconception: mistakes a ritual record for an artisan roster

options.text: It counted the tribute grain owed by a province that season
options.misconception: reads a divination text as a tax ledger

questions.explanation: Bone inscriptions recorded divination questions and omens. They were not contracts, rosters, or tax ledgers, though later readers may project those uses.
questions.hint: Focus on the act of cracking and asking.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: What a survival bias does to a claim
questions.learningObjective: Explain how survival bias weakens a historical claim
questions.stem: An engineer's design brief asks why surviving grant documents might overstate how common grants were

options.text: Because only successful grants were kept while failed ones were discarded
options.misconception: assumes discard without evidence of failure rates

options.text: Because grants were the only documents written in that period
options.misconception: overstates the exclusivity of grant writing

options.text: Because scribes copied grants more often than other documents
options.misconception: invents a copying preference not in the record

options.text: Because durable materials survived while perishable records of other acts did not

questions.explanation: Survival bias means durable records outlast perishable ones, so the sample skews toward what was written on lasting media. The tempting wrong idea assumes deliberate selection.

It replaced all family connections with purely random selection
options.misconception: exaggerates the break from kinship networks

options.text: It abolished the role of local officials in identifying talent
It guaranteed that every peasant could become an official

questions.explanation: Examinations added a merit-based route, not a total break from family influence. A overstates randomness, C overstates centralization, D confuses access with guarantee.
questions.hint: Focus on what new path appeared.

options.misconception: treats official source as neutral evidence

options.text: Reject it fully because all officials were biased and corrupt
Treat it as partial evidence shaped by the authors' own success
Ignore the record and rely only on modern estimates

questions.explanation: The claim has value but is shaped by the authors' interest in the system that advanced them. Neither full acceptance nor full rejection is warranted.

questions.explanation: Unification must first settle who holds authority where. Script, calendar, and religion follow political order rather than create it.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: Governing by grant in the early Zhou
questions.learningObjective: Explain why grants were given to relatives rather than strangers
questions.stem: An engineer's design brief asks why early Zhou grants went mostly to relatives of the king

answer.exemplar: Granting land to relatives reduced the risk of rebellion because kin shared family interest and reputation, making loyalty cheaper to secure than with strangers who owed no such bond.

questions.explanation: Kinship lowered the cost of trust. Relatives had shared reputation and family interest, so they were less likely to rebel than strangers with no bond.
questions.hint: Think about the cost of trust.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate whether a grant document is best read as a contract
questions.stem: An engineer's design brief asks whether reading a grant as a contract overstates its legal force

options.text: No, because both parties had stated duties and the document witnessed them
Yes, because the document only recorded a wish, not an enforceable duty
options.misconception: understates the reciprocal nature of the grant

options.text: Yes, because only the king had any power to enforce terms
options.misconception: ignores the lord's leverage through service

options.text: No, because the document was copied onto bronze for permanence

questions.explanation: The grant recorded mutual duties, so reading it as a contract is fair. Permanence of medium does not create force, and one-sided power does not erase reciprocity.
questions.hint: Look for duties on both sides.

questions.explanation: The bone records a question and a crack but no outcome, so weather favorability cannot be inferred. The other options are either supported or not contradicted.
questions.hint: Check what the bone actually records.

Treating it as a weather prediction

Treating it as a list of names only

questions.learningObjective: Explain why surviving records skew toward durable media
questions.stem: An engineer's design brief asks why surviving records skew toward durable media

answer.exemplar: Durable materials like bronze and bone resist decay, so records on them outlast perishable ones on wood or leather, skewing the sample toward what was written on lasting media.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: Identify a strength of an examination claim despite bias
